lines.text: Good evening, and welcome. The lights are low, and the shelves around you hold thousands of dark stones from the deserts of southern Peru.
Look closely at this one. A long-necked dinosaur. And beside it, a human being, hunting it. On another shelf, men perform heart surgery. On another, a man studies the sky through a telescope.
The man who built this collection believed these stones were a library left by a lost human race, older than the dinosaurs' extinction, who finally departed for the stars.
Tonight I am your audio guide. We will walk through the museum one room at a time. In each room, we hear what the stones are said to show, and then what the evidence says.
Seven rooms. One exit, where we sign the guestbook and give our verdict. Press play, and step inside.
Room one: the birthday stone. Our story begins in Ica, a desert town about three hundred kilometres south of Lima, on the thirteenth of May, nineteen sixty-six.

It is the forty-second birthday of a respected physician, Dr Javier Cabrera Darquea. His friend, the photographer Félix Llosa Romero, hands him a present: a small stone with a picture scratched into it.
Cabrera decides the picture shows a fish that has been extinct for millions of years. Which fish? He never said. Why extinct? He never explained. But from that moment, he was hooked.

Two brothers, Carlos and Pablo Soldi, had thousands of similar stones. They said a flood of the Ica River in nineteen sixty-one had washed them out of the ground near Ocucaje. Cabrera bought three hundred and forty-one.

Then he found a supplier who could bring him far more. A farmer named Basilio Uschuya. Over the following years, the stones arrived by the thousands. Remember that name. We will meet him again in room five.

Meanwhile, something happened that the legend rarely mentions. In nineteen sixty-six, the architect Santiago Agurto Calvo and the Ica museum curator Alejandro Pezzia dug in ancient cemeteries, and reported small engraved stones inside real tombs.
What did those stones show? A flower. A fish. A llama. No dinosaurs. No surgeons. Hold on to that difference. It is the most important clue in the building.
Room two: the dinosaurs. This is the room that made the museum famous. Long-necked giants, horned beasts, plated backs and flying reptiles.
People are shown hunting them, fighting them, even riding them. Fans point to one scene where hunters strike at a precise spot on a dinosaur's spine, as if they knew its anatomy.
If these were made by eyewitnesses, it would rewrite everything. Humans and dinosaurs together. Young-earth creationists still say so.

Now the evidence. The last non-avian dinosaurs died out about sixty-six million years ago. No dinosaur fossil has ever been dated to the age of humans, and no dinosaur remains are known around Ica at all.
And look at how they are drawn. The big meat-eater stands upright, its tail dragging on the ground. That is exactly how museums and films showed dinosaurs in the nineteen sixties.
Real eyewitnesses would have drawn the real animal. These stones drew the textbook of their own decade, including its mistakes.

Some meat-eaters have five fingers and five toes, which no fossil supports. Some stones show horned dinosaurs of a kind never found in South America. Others show dinosaurs hatching as larvae and changing shape like insects.
And here, a man rides a flying reptile like a horse. A real Pteranodon could never have lifted a human.
One more detail. The stones only show prehistoric animals that scientists already knew about in the nineteen sixties. Not a single new species. The library, it seems, was borrowed.
Room three: the surgeons. Cabrera was a doctor, and these were the stones he showed the world first. Heart transplants. Brain operations. Caesarean births. Kidney and liver transplants.
Supporters say only a culture with modern medicine could have drawn this.

But look at the surgeons. Big heads, long noses, loincloths and feather headdresses. In battle scenes they fight with axes and spears. A civilization that transplants hearts, but still fights with spears?

Now notice the timing. The first human heart transplant made world headlines in December nineteen sixty-seven, in Cape Town. The surgery stones became famous in the years right after. On its own, that proves nothing.
And there is a stranger detail, which we will hear in room five: one maker later said he engraved stones from drawings that Cabrera himself brought to him.
Skeptics also note how open these pictures are to reading. An open chest could be mutilation or a ritual, not a transplant.
Surgery stones, then, tell us a lot about the world of the nineteen sixties, and about the man who collected them. About ancient Peru, so far, they tell us very little.
Room four: the sky. Here are the astronomers. Men with what look like telescopes, watching comets. And flying machines.
One ancient mysteries author, David Hatcher Childress, joked that the telescope stone could just as easily show a game of prehistoric tennis. And many of the flying machines look a lot like birds.

Cabrera went much further. He wrote that the stones were made by Gliptolithic Man: humans with bigger brains, who used psychic energy to influence the heavens, and who existed at least four hundred and five million years ago.

Before a great comet struck, he said, they left Earth for a planet in the Pleiades, launching their craft from the plains of Nazca, which he called an ancient spaceport. And they had built the pyramids of Egypt along the way.

Ancient astronaut writers of the nineteen seventies, Erich von Däniken and Robert Charroux among them, carried the stones to a worldwide audience. The Nazca desert has its own disputed bodies, a separate case file.
But even among fringe writers, Cabrera's cosmic history found few followers. Over time, von Däniken himself concluded that many of the stones were most likely fakes.
Which brings us to the obvious question. If the stones were not made by sky people, who made them? For that, we have to leave the museum and visit a farm.
Room five: the workshop. This room is not in the museum at all. It is a farmhouse in Callango, in the Ica valley, home of Basilio Uschuya and his wife, Irma Gutiérrez.

In January nineteen seventy-five, a Peruvian magazine called Mundial published an interview with the couple. Every stone they had sold to Cabrera, they said, they had engraved themselves. The pictures came from comic books, school books and magazines.
Their tools were simple: knives, chisels, and a dentist's drill. The designs are not carved deep into the hard rock. They are scratched through a thin dark skin on the surface.
Then the aging. The fresh stones were baked in cow and donkey dung, and rubbed with boot polish, to darken the scratches.
Another time, Basilio described an easier recipe. Put the engraved stones in the chicken pen, he said, and the chickens did the rest.
In nineteen seventy-seven a BBC film crew came to Ica. Producer Ray Sutcliffe described Basilio as intelligent, proud of his work, with a great sense of humour.
For the camera, he took a fresh stone, switched on his drill, and engraved an ancient-looking picture in minutes. A simple stone can take about fifteen minutes.
Why do it? His answer was disarmingly honest. Making these stones, he said, is easier than farming the land.

There was a catch. Selling genuine Peruvian antiquities is illegal. After the BBC film, the authorities arrested Basilio. Under questioning he repeated it: the stones were his own work. He was released, and kept selling them, openly, as crafts.
He was not alone. Other local makers, including Pedro Huamán and Aparicio Aparcana, also admitted to engraving stones. Ica had a cottage industry.
Room six: the laboratory. Believers answered the confession with one strong argument: the stones are covered in an ancient patina. Surely that proves their age?
Here is the key. The stone itself can be very old. Andesite weathers slowly, forming a thin, soft rind. But the age of a stone is not the age of the picture scratched into it.

When the BBC's stone was examined in London, the rock looked ancient, but the edges of the engraving were clean and sharp, cut after the surface had weathered. Investigator Neil Steede saw the same thing: patina on the stone, none inside the grooves.
In the early nineteen nineties, stones examined in Barcelona showed traces of modern work: sandpaper, saws and acid.
What about Cabrera's own tests? He said a professor in Bonn and a mining engineer friend had confirmed the age. No laboratory report from Bonn has ever been produced.

Then came the clay. In nineteen ninety-seven, a German TV crew filmed a back room full of clay figurines: dinosaurs hatching from eggs, even kangaroos. Basilio said he had made those too. Clay, unlike stone, can be tested.
Von Däniken broke an arm off one figurine and sent it to a laboratory in Zurich. The answer: modern. Samples sent to Weimar came back relatively young, still containing water.
Supporters cite a two thousand three test dating a mineral crust on some stones to tens of thousands of years. It appeared in a believers' book, and it dates the crust, not the drawing.
Room seven: the locked door. Cabrera had an answer for everything. The farmer's stones, he said, were copies for tourists. Only twenty to forty fakes had slipped into his collection.
The real originals, he said, came from a secret cave near the Ica River, guarded by local people, holding a hoard of untouched stones. Nobody else was allowed to see it.
Investigator Neil Steede even offered to be blindfolded for the journey. He was refused, and concluded the cave never existed. No map, no photograph, no witness has ever surfaced.
Von Däniken once wrote that Cabrera had taken him to the cave. When Cabrera disputed it, von Däniken admitted he had made that part up.

And Basilio himself kept the mystery alive. In nineteen ninety-five he told Steede that he had engraved stones from Cabrera's drawings, but that Cabrera also owned about five thousand stones he had not made. Later he even claimed his confession was only to stay out of prison.

So could any stones be genuine? Possibly a few, like the small ones from real tombs, with flowers, fish, birds and llamas, finer and shallower. A Spanish report from the sixteenth century is also said to mention engraved stones. But none shows a dinosaur.
And here is the honest gap. No one has ever done an independent study to separate possibly ancient stones from modern ones. Behind this door, a real question is still waiting.
Our tour is over. On the way out, let us sign the guestbook.

Andesite pebbles with a soft weathered skin: evidence. Makers who confessed and demonstrated on film: evidence. Dinosaurs drawn like nineteen sixties museum models: evidence. A few plain motifs that may be truly ancient: possible.
Humans living alongside dinosaurs: debunked. Gliptolithic Man and alien knowledge: no evidence. Exactly who engraved all fifty thousand stones: still open.

The verdict. The famous dinosaur, surgery and telescope stones are modern engravings, made for sale from the nineteen sixties onward by farmers of the Ica valley, and read by a sincere doctor into a cosmic myth. No lost race. No alien library.
What stays open is smaller and more human: which plain stones might be truly ancient, and how much the collector shaped the pictures he was sold.

Cabrera called his stones the most important legacy of our time. In a way, he was right. They are a perfect record of the nineteen sixties: its dinosaurs, its heart surgeons, its space age dreams, scratched into ancient rock.
Thank you for visiting. Which room changed your mind? Tell us in the comments, and subscribe for the next ancient mystery put to the test.
